newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen soft in late Europe, dlr/mark near high.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen soft in late Europe, dlr/mark near high.

text.p: The dollar was mixed by late Europe trade, softer against the yen after some dollar-dampening comments out of Japan but with dollar/mark near its session high after a day of range-trading.
The dollar got a lift in Europe's afternoon trade from stronger-than-expected U.S. industrial production data.

But against the yen, it soon shed these mild gains as dealers were nervous following comments earlier in the day from Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's international finance bureau, warning about excessive moves in the currency market.
The dollar was at 125.70/80 yen at 1522 GMT, down from 126.23/33 in late European trade on Tuesday. Against the mark, it was at 1.7272/77 against Tuesday's 1.7318/23.

The market was now poised for Japanese trade data due at 2350 GMT today and U.S. trade data due on Thursday, dealers said, particularly since the politically sensitive US-Japan trade issue has emerged to the fore again recently.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Wednesday that the United States was concerned about its trade imbalance with Japan and that it did not want to see the gap grow wider.

This follows a comment made earlier this month by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who during a visit to Tokyo expressed concerns about the US-Japan trade gap but also said currencies should not be used as instruments of trade policy.
Dollar/yen sentiment was dampened meanwhile by Sakakibara's comment, which came during Europe's morning trade, that Japan would intervene when "we think we can win".
"Sakakibara has underlined that intervention is very much on the minds of the Japanese authorities," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS in London.

"With the size of the (dollar) reserves the Bank of Japan would have that it could throw into intervention, the market is cautious, given at the moment the lack of fresh factors to send dollar/yen higher," Lambert said.
But he said, and others agreed, that the dollar's underlying bullish sentiment was still intact.

"It's difficult to come up with reasons why the dollar shouldn't gain on the yen, even though the Japanese trade surplus is higher and the U.S. has started to mutter a bit more about it," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe.
"People don't think the U.S. government wants to control underlying (dollar) direction," Fishwick said.
Meanwhile, the mark was range-bound against other European currencies, unmoved by a series of comments related to European monetary union.
Italian financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore cited sources in Bonn saying a deal was taking shape between Germany and France to leave Italy and Spain out of the first round of EMU in 1999.
Top-level European officials denied the report, with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi saying there were no such "secret deals".
Waigel also said Germany still had a chance of meeting the three percent budget deficit-to-GDP ratio required for EMU membership, and dismissed speculation of a relaxation of this criterion.

The British pound was softer against the mark and dollar, though off its session lows, after UK jobs and earnings data dampened concern about an overheating labour market. Sterling was at 2.8063/73 marks and $1.6234/40 against late Tuesday's 2.8193/03 and $1.6258/68.
